families.title: Spring-water Jugs full jugs
families.mathematics: Pouring only full jugs of sizes a and b into a tank, and taking jugfuls back out, fills exactly the levels ia + jb with whole i, j ≥ 0: the numerical semigroup generated by a and b. If a and b share a factor g > 1, every level is a multiple of g, so infinitely many levels never fill. If they share none, every level after ab − a − b fills and ab − a − b does not (Sylvester, 1884), and exactly (a − 1)(b − 1)/2 levels never fill. A run of a filled levels in a row, a the smaller jug, certifies that every later level fills, because one more jug of a repeats the run. Two ways to fill the same level differ by trading b jugs of a for a jugs of b. The base jugs, which pour from one jug into another, measure any multiple of g; here nothing is poured between jugs, which is why small levels are the hard ones.
rules: Pour empties one full jug into the tank. − takes one jugful back out.
A level is filled when the water sits exactly on its line. It lights up.
The order of the jugfuls does not matter.

sources.title: Bellingham Math Circle — Week 29: Two-length builders, packets and adult guide

If you go over, take a jugful back.

parent.notice: Which pairs your child tries, and whether they look for where the dark levels stop.
parent.prompt: Which pair leaves the most dark levels before the row turns all light?
parent.explanation: Jugs a and b fill the levels ia + jb. If they share a factor, the gaps never stop; otherwise the last gap is ab − a − b.
parent.extension: Find a pair whose last gap is more than 30.
parent.connection: Sylvester (1884): with coprime a and b, the largest level that never fills is ab − a − b, and half of the levels below it fill.

puzzles.title: Ten
puzzles.objective: Fill the tank exactly to 10 with full 3-jugs and 4-jugs.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill the tank to the line.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the tank exactly to 10 with full 3-jugs and 4-jugs.

rules: Pour empties one full jug into the tank. − takes one jugful back out.
A level is filled when the water sits exactly on its line. It lights up.
The order of the jugfuls does not matter.
puzzles.idea: 10 = 3 + 3 + 4: a level can mix both jugs.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count up to 10. Nothing to read but numbers.
hints: Pour a jug and watch where the water stops.
Three 3-jugs make 9 and two 4-jugs make 8. Try mixing.
Pour two 3-jugs and one 4-jug: 3 + 3 + 4 = 10.

parent.notice: Whether your child adjusts after going over, taking a jugful back rather than starting again.
parent.prompt: What happened when you went past the line?
parent.explanation: Only full jugs go in, so the tank holds 3s and 4s added up. 3 + 3 + 4 = 10 is the only way; 3s alone give 9 or 12 and 4s alone give 8 or 12.
parent.extension: Which levels below 10 can these jugs fill?
parent.connection: The levels these jugs fill are the sums 3i + 4j, with i and j whole numbers: a numerical semigroup.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 launch (3 + 4 = 7) and K–1 Problem 1 (10 = 3 + 3 + 4 with 3-rods and 4-rods).

puzzles.title: Three and four
puzzles.objective: Fill every level from 1 to 12 that the 3-jug and the 4-jug can, then press That’s all.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill every level you can, then press That’s all.
puzzles.instruction: Fill every level from 1 to 12 that the 3-jug and the 4-jug can, then press That’s all.
puzzles.controls: Tap a level to set the line. Pour empties a full jug into the tank; − takes one jugful back out; Empty pours the tank away. Press That’s all when no other level can be filled.
rules: Pour empties one full jug into the tank. − takes one jugful back out.
A level is filled when the water sits exactly on its line. It lights up.
The order of the jugfuls does not matter.
That’s all says no other level in the row can be filled with these jugs. A wrong claim is refused.
puzzles.idea: 3 and 4 miss only 1, 2 and 5; from 6 on, every level fills.
hints: Fill every level you can first.
Is there a way to make 5 out of 3s and 4s?
Light every level but 1, 2 and 5, then press That’s all.

parent.notice: Whether your child explains 5: one 3 leaves 2, one 4 leaves 1, and two of anything is too much.
parent.explanation: Levels 1 and 2 are smaller than either jug. Level 5 would need a 3 and then 2 more, or a 4 and then 1 more, and neither is a jug. From 6 on, 6 = 3 + 3, 7 = 3 + 4 and 8 = 4 + 4 start a run of three, and one more 3 carries each of them on forever.
parent.extension: With 3 and 5, which levels can’t be filled?
parent.connection: The levels that never fill are the gaps of the semigroup; 3 and 4 have (3 − 1)(4 − 1)/2 = 3 of them.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 K–1 Problems 1 and 4 and grades 2–3 Problem 1 (3-rods and 4-rods, lengths 1 to 16).

puzzles.title: Every way to twelve
puzzles.objective: Find every way to fill the tank to 12 with full 3-jugs and 4-jugs, then press That’s all.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find every way to fill 12, then press That’s all.

puzzles.controls: Pour empties a full jug into the tank; − takes one jugful back out; Empty pours the tank away. Each new way joins the list. Press That’s all when there is no other way.
rules: Pour empties one full jug into the tank. − takes one jugful back out.
A level is filled when the water sits exactly on its line. It lights up.
The order of the jugfuls does not matter.
Each different way to fill the level (how many of each jug) is listed once. That’s all says there is no other way. A wrong claim is refused.
puzzles.idea: 12 is four 3s or three 4s, and nothing in between.
hints: Each new way joins the list.
Try one 4-jug and then 3s. Then two 4-jugs.
Four 3s and three 4s; one or two 4s leave 8 or 4, which 3s cannot make.

parent.notice: Whether your child checks the mixed cases (one or two 4s) before saying there is no third way.
parent.explanation: One 4 leaves 8 and two 4s leave 4, neither a multiple of 3. So 12 is four 3s or three 4s.
parent.extension: How many ways are there to fill 24?
parent.connection: Four 3s and three 4s both make 12, so swapping one group for the other turns any way into another.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 K–1 Problem 2 and grades 2–3 Problem 2 (every way to make 12 with 3-rods and 4-rods).

puzzles.title: Three and five

puzzles.idea: 3 and 5 miss 1, 2, 4 and 7, and then never again.
hints: Fill every level you can first.
Try 7: one 5 leaves 2, and 3s leave 1 or 4.
Light every level but 1, 2, 4 and 7, then press That’s all.

parent.notice: Whether your child sees that 8, 9 and 10 in a row settle every later level.
parent.prompt: After 7, could a level ever fail again?
parent.explanation: 7 fails: no 5 leaves 7, one 5 leaves 2, and 3s give 3, 6. Then 8 = 3 + 5, 9 = 3 + 3 + 3 and 10 = 5 + 5, and adding 3s to these three reaches every later level.
parent.extension: Where do the gaps stop for 4 and 5?
parent.connection: 3 · 5 − 3 − 5 = 7 is the last level that never fills, and (3 − 1)(5 − 1)/2 = 4 levels never fill.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 K–1 Problem 3 and grades 2–3 Problem 3 (3-rods and 5-rods, the impossible lengths to 20).

Each different way to fill the level (how many of each jug) is listed once. That’s all says there is no other way. A wrong claim is refused.
puzzles.idea: Eight 3s, four 3s and three 4s, or six 4s: each way trades four 3s for three 4s.
hints: Each new way joins the list.
Four 3s and three 4s both make 12.
The three ways are eight 3s, four 3s with three 4s, and six 4s.

parent.notice: Whether your child finds one way from another by swapping four 3s for three 4s.
parent.prompt: How can you change one way into another?
parent.explanation: The number of 4s must leave a multiple of 3, so it is 0, 3 or 6, giving eight 3s, four 3s and three 4s, or six 4s. Each step swaps four 3s (12) for three 4s (12).
parent.extension: How many ways are there to fill 36?
parent.connection: Any two ways to fill a level with jugs a and b differ by whole trades of b jugs of a for a jugs of b, when a and b share no factor.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 grades 2–3 Problem 2 and grades 4–5 Problem 6 (every way to build 24, and the replacement that changes one into another).

puzzles.idea: 2 and 3, 2 and 5, and 3 and 4 work; 2 and 4 miss the odd levels, 3 and 5 miss 7, and 4 and 5 miss 6, 7 and 11.
hints: Tap two jugs at the top.
Two even jugs can only make even levels.
Try the 3-jug and the 4-jug.

parent.notice: Whether your child rules a pair out by one failing level, then tries another.
parent.prompt: Which pairs fail, and at which level?
parent.explanation: Three pairs fill every level from 6 to 12: 2 and 3, 2 and 5, and 3 and 4. 2 and 4 make only even levels (7, 9 and 11 fail), 3 and 5 miss 7, and 4 and 5 miss 6, 7 and 11.
parent.extension: Which pair has the most levels that never fill?
parent.connection: A pair with a common factor misses infinitely many levels; a pair without one misses only (a − 1)(b − 1)/2.

puzzles.title: Where the gaps stop
puzzles.objective: Find the last level the 4-jug and the 5-jug can’t fill. Show it by filling the levels after it, then claim it.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find the last level that can’t be filled.
puzzles.instruction: Find the last level the 4-jug and the 5-jug can’t fill. Show it by filling the levels after it, then claim it.
puzzles.controls: Tap a level to set the line. Pour empties a full jug into the tank; − takes one jugful back out; Empty pours the tank away. With a level chosen, “Last gap is …” claims it; “Gaps never stop” claims there is no last gap.
rules: Pour empties one full jug into the tank. − takes one jugful back out.
A level is filled when the water sits exactly on its line. It lights up.
The order of the jugfuls does not matter.

“Last gap is …” says the chosen level can’t be filled and every later level can; it is accepted when the levels just after it are lit. “Gaps never stop” says infinitely many levels can’t be filled. A wrong claim is refused.
puzzles.idea: 11 can’t be filled, and 12, 13, 14 and 15 can: four in a row with a 4-jug means every later level can too.
hints: Fill the levels you can and look for where the gaps stop.
How many filled levels in a row are enough, when one more 4 repeats them?
Fill 12, 13, 14 and 15, choose 11, and press Last gap.

parent.notice: Whether your child sees why four filled levels in a row settle every later one.
parent.prompt: If 12, 13, 14 and 15 fill, how do you fill 16? And 17?
parent.explanation: 11 fails: no 5s leave 11, one 5 leaves 6, two leave 1, and none of those is a pile of 4s. 12 = 4 + 4 + 4, 13 = 4 + 4 + 5, 14 = 4 + 5 + 5 and 15 = 5 + 5 + 5. Every later level is one of these plus some 4s.
parent.extension: Find the last gap for 4 and 7.
parent.connection: 4 · 5 − 4 − 5 = 11. The claim is checked with a finite certificate: a run as long as the smaller jug.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 grades 2–3 Problem 4 and grades 4–5 Problem 2 (the last impossible length for 4 and 5, with a finite collection of builds that settles every longer target).

puzzles.title: Four and seven
puzzles.objective: Find the last level the 4-jug and the 7-jug can’t fill, or say the gaps never stop.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find the last level that can’t be filled.
puzzles.instruction: Find the last level the 4-jug and the 7-jug can’t fill, or say the gaps never stop.

rules: Pour empties one full jug into the tank. − takes one jugful back out.
A level is filled when the water sits exactly on its line. It lights up.
The order of the jugfuls does not matter.

“Last gap is …” says the chosen level can’t be filled and every later level can; it is accepted when the levels just after it are lit. “Gaps never stop” says infinitely many levels can’t be filled. A wrong claim is refused.
puzzles.idea: 17 is the last gap: 18, 19, 20 and 21 fill, and 17 minus any number of 7s is never a pile of 4s.
hints: Look for four filled levels in a row.
Try 17: take away no 7s, one or two. What is left?
Fill 18, 19, 20 and 21, choose 17, and press Last gap.

parent.notice: Whether your child checks 17 by taking away 7s (17, 10, 3) rather than by guessing.
parent.explanation: 17, 10 and 3 (17 with no, one or two 7s taken away) are none of them multiples of 4, so 17 fails. 18 = 4 + 7 + 7, 19 = 4 + 4 + 4 + 7, 20 = 4 · 5 and 21 = 7 · 3, and adding 4s reaches every later level. 13 also fails.
parent.extension: Predict the last gap for 5 and 7.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 grades 2–3 Problem 5 and grades 4–5 Problems 3–4 (4-rods and 7-rods: the last impossible length, and 17).

puzzles.title: Four and six
puzzles.objective: Find the last level the 4-jug and the 6-jug can’t fill, or say the gaps never stop.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find the last level that can’t be filled.
puzzles.instruction: Find the last level the 4-jug and the 6-jug can’t fill, or say the gaps never stop.

“Last gap is …” says the chosen level can’t be filled and every later level can; it is accepted when the levels just after it are lit. “Gaps never stop” says infinitely many levels can’t be filled. A wrong claim is refused.
puzzles.idea: Both jugs are even, so every odd level stays empty forever: the gaps never stop.
hints: Fill every level you can first.
What do all the filled levels have in common?
Every filled level is even. Press Gaps never stop.

parent.notice: Whether your child gives the reason (4 and 6 are both even) rather than only noticing a pattern.
parent.prompt: Could an odd level ever fill?
parent.explanation: Every jugful adds an even amount, so every level the tank can reach is even, and no odd level ever fills. Level 2 fails too, because both jugs are bigger than 2. Every even level from 4 on fills.
parent.extension: Which pairs of jugs have gaps that never stop?
parent.connection: With jugs a and b the filled levels are all multiples of their greatest common factor; the gaps stop exactly when that factor is 1.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 grades 2–3 Problem 6 and grades 4–5 Problem 5 (pairs with infinitely many impossible lengths, including 4 and 6).

“Last gap is …” says the chosen level can’t be filled and every later level can; it is accepted when the levels just after it are lit. “Gaps never stop” says infinitely many levels can’t be filled. A wrong claim is refused.
puzzles.idea: 23 is the last gap, and five levels in a row, 24 to 28, prove it.
hints: Now you need five filled levels in a row.
Try 23: take away no 7s, one, two or three. What is left?
Fill 24 to 28, choose 23, and press Last gap.

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts the last gap from the earlier pairs before filling.
parent.prompt: The last gaps so far were 5, 7, 11 and 17. What do you predict for 5 and 7?
parent.explanation: 23, 16, 9 and 2 are not multiples of 5, so 23 fails. 24 = 5 + 5 + 7 + 7, 25 = 5 · 5, 26 = 5 + 7 · 3, 27 = 5 · 4 + 7 and 28 = 7 · 4, and adding 5s reaches every later level.
parent.extension: Choose two jugs whose last gap is 11.
parent.connection: Sylvester’s formula: with jugs a and b sharing no factor, the last gap is ab − a − b = 35 − 12 = 23.

puzzles.provenance: Week 29 grades 4–5 Problem 7 (predict and test the last impossible length for 5-rods and 7-rods).

puzzles.title: Last gap eleven
puzzles.objective: Choose two jugs from 2 to 9 whose last level that can’t be filled is 11, and show it.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Choose two jugs whose last gap is 11.
puzzles.instruction: Choose two jugs from 2 to 9 whose last level that can’t be filled is 11, and show it.
puzzles.controls: Tap two jugs at the top to choose them, then tap a level to set the line. Pour empties a full jug into the tank; − takes one jugful back out; Empty pours the tank away. Press “Last gap is …” when the claim is ready.
rules: Pour empties one full jug into the tank. − takes one jugful back out.
A level is filled when the water sits exactly on its line. It lights up.
The order of the jugfuls does not matter.
Tap two jugs at the top to choose them. The claim is accepted when the level can’t be filled and the levels just after it are lit.
puzzles.idea: 3 and 7, or 4 and 5: both have last gap 11.
hints: Tap two jugs, then fill the levels after 11.
You have seen a pair with last gap 11.
Choose the 4-jug and the 5-jug, fill 12 to 15, and press Last gap.

parent.notice: Whether your child uses earlier pairs (4 and 5 from puzzle 7) or the rule ab − a − b to aim.
parent.prompt: Which pair from before had 11 as its last gap?
parent.explanation: With jugs sharing no factor the last gap is ab − a − b, so (a − 1)(b − 1) = 12. From 2 to 9 that gives 3 and 7 (2 · 6) and 4 and 5 (3 · 4). 2 and 13 also works, but 13 is not offered.
parent.extension: Is there a pair whose last gap is 12?
parent.connection: ab − a − b = (a − 1)(b − 1) − 1, so with coprime jugs the last gap plus 1 is always an even product.

puzzles.provenance: New, after Week 29 grades 4–5 Problems 7–8 (propose a rule for the last gap; invent two coprime lengths).

puzzles.title: Last gap thirteen
puzzles.objective: Choose two jugs from 2 to 12 whose last level that can’t be filled is 13, and show it.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Choose two jugs whose last gap is 13.
puzzles.instruction: Choose two jugs from 2 to 12 whose last level that can’t be filled is 13, and show it.
puzzles.controls: Tap two jugs at the top to choose them, then tap a level to set the line. Pour empties a full jug into the tank; − takes one jugful back out; Empty pours the tank away. Press “Last gap is …” when the claim is ready.
rules: Pour empties one full jug into the tank. − takes one jugful back out.
A level is filled when the water sits exactly on its line. It lights up.
The order of the jugfuls does not matter.
Tap two jugs at the top to choose them. The claim is accepted when the level can’t be filled and the levels just after it are lit.
puzzles.idea: Only 3 and 8 work among these jugs: (3 − 1)(8 − 1) = 14.
hints: Tap two jugs, then fill the levels after 13.
With the 2-jug, the last gap is 2 less than the other jug, so the 2-jug can’t work here.
Choose the 3-jug and the 8-jug, fill 14, 15 and 16, and press Last gap.

parent.notice: Whether your child searches pairs or reasons from (a − 1)(b − 1) = 14.
parent.prompt: What does 13 + 1 = 14 tell you about the jugs?
parent.explanation: (a − 1)(b − 1) = 14 gives 2 and 15 or 3 and 8, and only 3 and 8 are offered. 13 fails with 3 and 8 (13, 5 are not multiples of 3), and 14 = 3 · 2 + 8, 15 = 3 · 5 and 16 = 8 · 2.
parent.extension: Why is there no pair with last gap 12?
parent.connection: For coprime a and b the last gap is (a − 1)(b − 1) − 1, and one of a, b is odd unless both are even (then they share 2), so (a − 1)(b − 1) is even and the last gap is odd.
